chunks.text: So you can see we begin with these general purpose registers.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So you have these general purpose registers, which you can see if you use them combinedly, AH and AL combinedly are called as AX. BH and BL are combinedly called as BX.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: And similarly, this is CX and DX.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So you can say that you have four general purpose registers of 16-bit each, right?

chunks.text: Or alternatively, you can say that if you see them as 8-bit registers, you have got A higher, A lower, B higher, B lower and so on and so forth.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So you have got eight general purpose registers of 8-bit each or 1-byte each.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So you can say that you have got one word registers, which are four in number.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: One word means two bytes.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So you have got four one word registers or alternatively, you have got eight one byte registers or alternatively, you may use any combination between them.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: You can use this BX register as a whole as 16-bit and maybe CL register as only 8-bit registers.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So we have got these general purpose registers here.

chunks.text: However, later on, we will see that the CX register is usually used for counter operation.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: And every register has a specific purpose.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Another important point to note here is that the accumulator now here is little bit free of responsibilities as it was in 8-0-8-5.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Because in 8-0-8-5, whatever calculation happens inside the microprocessor, the result of that will be by default stored in the accumulator.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: But here it will not happen.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Here the result will be stored in the register in which we will specify.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Right.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So in that way, this accumulator is little bit free as compared to 8-0-8-5.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: But it is still called as accumulator because for some default calculations, it is still used as a default register.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Right.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: But not for all of the calculations as it was the case in 8-0-8-5 microprocessor.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Now, after general purpose registers, we have got these index registers.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Index registers means the full form of this is source index and this is destination index, SI and DI.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So let me first discuss the segment registers and then we will discuss these index registers, pointer registers and control registers.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So segment registers, these are again 16-bit registers.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Right.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So what are they used for?

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: In 8-0-8-6 microprocessor, the externally interfaced memory is of 1 megabyte.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: And we said that inside that 1 megabyte memory, you are free to create your code segment, your data segment, your stack segment and your extra segment.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So since the memory is of 1 megabyte, we have got 20 bits, 20 bit of address for every location.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So in 20 bits or in hexadecimal, we can say that 5 hexadecimal digits address will be there for every external memory location.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: But there is a foundation on the starting address of code segment, data segment, stack segment and extra segment.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: If you see the hexadecimal representation, the address will be of 5 hexadecimal digits for the externally interfaced memory.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: And the foundation for starting address of code segment, data segment, stack segment and extra segment in the external memory is that the last hexadecimal digit has to be 0.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Or the least significant hexadecimal digit has to be 0 for that case.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Right.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So that way we are only left with 16 bits.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: And inside the microprocessor to hold the starting address of that, we have got these 16 bit segment registers.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Code segment, data segment, stack segment and extra segment.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So this is not the code segment.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: This is a register which keeps the first 16 bits address out of the 20 bits of code segment.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Right.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Because the least significant 4 bits are by default 0.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: This is a restriction in 8086.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: And wherever you start your segment from, it has to begin in that way.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So these segment registers are used for that particular purpose.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So these are 16 bit registers.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So they consume 4 hexadecimal digits.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: And if you want to take the starting address of any segment, you have to append an extra hexadecimal digit, which is 0 after these segment registers.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Now, in combination with this segment registers, we use index registers.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: For example, we are working in data segment.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So suppose the actual physical address of the data segment is 50,000 in hexadecimal.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Right.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: 50,000 in hexadecimal.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So last hexadecimal digit has to be 0, which it is in 50,000.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: The last digit is already 0.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So this data segment will keep 5,000 in itself.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: 5,000 in hexadecimal in itself.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Data segment register, which is internet to microprocessor.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: The remaining 0 is implicit.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So this data segment will contain that particular address.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Now, inside the data segment, you have got 64 kilobyte of memory in the externally interfaced memory, starting from location 50,000.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: And after that, you consume 64 kilobyte locations.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So that complete section will be called as your data segment.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: In that data segment, if you want to navigate, you have got this source index and destination index register.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Right.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So this source index and destination index register is nothing.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: But after this initial 50,000, where we are going inside the data segment, it can be kept here.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Suppose I want to access a location of 50,000 for 5004.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So data segment will contain 5000 because it is a 16-bit register.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: And a 0 is implicit after that in hexadecimal because it is a constraint.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: And this source index may contain 0004.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: 0004 because every segment is of 64 kilobyte.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So to be able to address every location inside the 64 kilobyte, you only need 16-bit addresses.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So that is why this segment index, it contains the offset.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: It contains actually the index of locations within that 64 kilobyte segment.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So this SI will contain 0004.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: DS will contain 5000.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So if we want to calculate the actual address from DS and SI, what we will do is we will take 5000,

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: append a 0 after that so that it will become 50,000 in hexadecimal.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: And then SI register already contains 0004.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So we will add it to that.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So it will become 500004.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So that is the way we calculate these addresses.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So we have got the actual physical address.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Then we have got base address, which is kept in this DS register, which is the beginning of any segment.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: And then inside that we have got this logical address.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: SI contains the logical address.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Now implementing addresses in this way is important because if you somehow try to change the starting of data segment in your program.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Right.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So you can simply just change the content of this DS register.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: REST program will remain same because SI works on relative address.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: The value that you will keep in SI will be related to DS.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So even if you change the value of DS in your program, this SI does not need to be changed because SI is already related to DS.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So we will see this when we will see an example of coding.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: So there it will become more clear to all of us.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Then similarly for DS, you have got this SI and DI pairs.

chunks.text: Right.

chunks.text: Instruction pointer, which is a control register, it is used for code segment.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Why is it called as control register?

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Because CS and IP, the combination of CS and IP will contain, it will contain the address of next instruction to be executed.

chunks.title: Video 13 - 8086 Programming Model
chunks.text: Right.

chunks.text: So I told you in the beginning that instruction pointer is similar to program counter in 8085, but not instruction pointer alone.

chunks.text: So we will have a combination of code segment, segment register plus instruction pointer.

chunks.text: Because CS, when we will apply a zero after that, and then we will add the value of IP in that, we will get the actual physical address of the next instruction to be executed.
